column2: Samson goes from there to Gaza, sees a harlot and goes in to her; the sexual encounter remains in the restrained source idiom.
The warning, surrounding and gate ambush retain both all-night expressions and the proposed morning killing.
column3: The place is an English supplied object for surrounded; the Greek does not specify a named building here.

column2: Midnight is repeated; doors, two posts and bar go onto his shoulder and up to the mountain facing Hebron, where he sets them down.
Samson's love for Delilah is placed after the preceding events and beside the Sorek torrent; no marriage or ethnicity is added for her.
The satraps seek deception, discovery, victory, binding and humiliation, each promising eleven hundred silver pieces; the amount remains per man rather than a group total.
Delilah asks both where the strength lies and how he can be bound for humiliation; the stated hostile purpose is retained.
The first condition specifies seven moist, undried sinew-strings, followed by weakness and ordinary human likeness.
column3: Any other man renders one of the humans idiomatically, without asserting that Samson is nonhuman.

column2: The satraps supply the same seven undried sinew-strings and Delilah binds him; the repeated material description remains.
The ambush group waits in the inner room; the first foreigners warning precedes broken strings, the fire-smelling flax image and undisclosed strength.
Behold marks her charge of deception and false speech, followed by the renewed binding question; both accusations remain.
Seven new cords never used for work distinguish the second claim; tightly voices the emphatic binding construction, followed by the repeated weakness claim.
column3: Tightly is an interpretive rendering of desmo desosin; emphatic indeed bind is a less physically specific alternative.

column2: New cords, the repeated warning, the waiting ambush and the thread comparison remain; the cords break from his arms.
Her until-now accusation leads to a seven-strand weaving condition with a singular peg and wall; the full selected concluding weakness clause remains.
Delilah puts him to sleep and weaves seven curls, this time using plural pegs; his waking pulls out pegs, fabric and warp, followed by undisclosed strength.
column3: Loom terminology and the precise objects of drove and tore require specialist lexical review; no shorter witness is substituted.

column2: The love claim contrasts with a heart not with her and the third deception; I love you gives the present force of the perfect-form profession.
Her speech wears him down all night, not many days; his faintheartedness reaches the point of death.
column3: Grew weary for oligopsycheo remains provisional, as at 10:16; the context here includes sustained harassment.

column2: No razor shall come preserves the selected future prohibition, with Nazirite identity from his mother's womb and three consequences of shaving.
Delilah recognizes full disclosure, calls all the satraps, and all the satrapies come carrying silver; the unusual change of noun is retained.
column3: Satrapies is a source-visible collective/metonymic expression, not a claim that geographical territories literally walk; glossary and literary assessment remain open.

column2: Sleep between her knees, the barber's summons, seven curls removed and ensuing humiliation and lost strength remain.
column3: Had the curls shaved makes Delilah causally responsible without deciding whether she or the barber is the grammatical subject of exyresen; that subject is not separately expressed.

column2: Propose go out and act as I always do to represent both exeleusomai and poieso, with aei retained as always; the shake-free intention and ignorance of the Lord's departure remain.
column3: Free expresses the contextual result of shaking himself; it is not a separate object in the Greek.

column2: Capture, eyes dug out, descent to Gaza, bronze fetters and prison grinding remain in order.
column3: Grain supplies the contextual object of grinding; the selected clause does not separately name what was ground.

column2: Hair begins to grow after shaving; again expresses contextual regrowth, without claiming a separate renewed-action word in Greek.
Satraps gather to sacrifice greatly to Dagon and rejoice, attributing Samson's capture to their god in quoted speech.
The people praise their gods in the plural but speak of our god in the singular; the enemy, land devastation and increased casualties remain.
column3: Slain for traumatias is unresolved. The accessible Perseus vocabulary gloss gives wounded man (https://vocab.perseus.org/word-list/urn%3Acts%3AgreekLit%3Atlg2703.tlg001.opp-grc1%3A5/?o=3&page=all, accessed 2026-11-13), but that general gloss alone does not settle fatal versus nonfatal casualties in this LXX context. Full LSJ/Logeion entry access was unsuccessful; no such entry review is credited.

column2: Their merry heart prompts a request for Samson to perform, but their subsequent action is mocking him; both activities and placement between two pillars remain.
Samson asks the hand-leading boy for rest and tactile access to the supporting pillars so he can lean; the selected notice that the boy complied remains.
The full house, all satraps and about three thousand men and women on the roof remain distinct groups and locations.
The double Lord address, remember and strengthen requests, just-this-once-more limitation and one vengeance for two eyes all remain.
column3: No archaic pronoun is required where the direct prayer contains only imperatives; the selected one vengeance is not changed to vengeance for one eye.

column2: Samson embraces the two middle supporting pillars and leans, one at each hand; the right/left distinction remains.
Let my soul die preserves the life-language of the request; strong bending brings the house onto rulers and people, and deaths exceed those caused in his life.
Brothers and the whole paternal household retrieve and bury Samson between Zorah and Eshtaol in Manoah's tomb; twenty years of judging is repeated.
Micah is introduced as a man of Ephraim's hill country; no relationship to a later prophet is suggested.
Micah admits taking eleven hundred silver pieces after hearing his mother's adjuration; behold introduces possession and her blessing follows.
column3: Adjuration preserves exorkizo's oath-related wording without inserting the contents of a curse; blessed of the Lord is inherited traditional English for the dative relationship.

column2: The full eleven hundred is returned; the mother emphatically consecrates it separately for carved and cast images, then promises both return them and give it back.
column3: The plural-to-singular object shift and separately for kata monas remain visible; neither an omitted son-beneficiary nor a harmonized pronoun is supplied.

column2: The return is repeated; two hundred pieces go to the caster for the images placed in Micah's house, without inventing a disposition for the remainder.
Micah's house of God, ephod and teraphim precede filling one son's hand to make him priest; the installation image remains.
column3: Filled the hand is an idiom for priestly installation here; a reader glossary is preferable to erasing the source image or implying merely a cash payment.

column2: The no-king notice is paired with each man's doing what is good in his own eyes; good retains the selected adjective without narrator endorsement.
The young man's Bethlehem/Judah district and Judah kinship are stated alongside Levite identity and sojourning; the apparent tension is not repaired.
He leaves Bethlehem to seek a place to sojourn and reaches Micah's house while traveling through Ephraim's hill country.
column3: A place supplies the understood object of find in ordinary English, not an additional geographical identification.

column2: His answer repeats Levite identity, Bethlehem of Judah and the open-ended search for residence; the repetition remains.
Micah proposes fatherhood and priesthood, ten silver pieces for the year, a pair of garments and living provisions; the Levite's movement continues into verse 11.
column3: For the year interprets eis hemeras as a recurring annual period; the literal days expression and possible payment-period alternatives require further lexical review.

column2: The Levite begins residing with Micah and becomes like one of his sons, preserving the contrast with father in Micah's offer.
Micah fills the Levite's hand, making him his priest in his house; the repeated installation idiom remains consistent with verse 5.
Micah says the Lord has done good to him because the Levite became his priest; the selected past action is not changed into a promise of future prosperity.
